# Advanced Navigation Topics

## Why This Chapter Exists

This chapter is a brief tour of topics that sit beyond the required course
projects. These are not new assignment requirements, and students will not be
assessed on implementing them. The goal is professional awareness: if you keep
working in autonomous navigation, these are the ideas, acronyms, and research
directions you will keep seeing.

The course projects emphasize implementable foundations: filtering, visual
navigation, FastSLAM, and loose INS/GNSS integration. Modern navigation systems
build on those foundations, but they often use more complex optimization,
multi-sensor fusion, raw GNSS processing, learned perception, and resilience
methods for environments where one sensor cannot be trusted.

Think of this chapter as a map of the neighborhood, not a demand that you build
the entire city by Friday.

## Factor Graphs and Smoothing

Many modern navigation systems are written as optimization problems rather than
only as recursive filters. Instead of estimating only the current state, a
smoothing system estimates a window or full history of states. Measurements become
factors that constrain those states.

Common factors include:

- IMU preintegration between keyframes;
- camera reprojection residuals;
- lidar or radar scan-matching residuals;
- GNSS pseudorange, Doppler, carrier phase, or position factors;
- wheel odometry, barometer, magnetometer, or terrain constraints;
- loop-closure constraints between revisited locations.

The graph view is powerful because it treats heterogeneous measurements in one
consistent framework. A visual-inertial-GNSS smoother, for example, can contain
camera factors, IMU factors, GNSS factors, and prior factors in the same
least-squares problem.

This does not make filtering obsolete. Filters are still useful when memory,
latency, or certification constraints are tight. Smoothing is attractive when
past states should be revisited, as in loop closure, bundle adjustment, and
post-processing. Many deployed systems use both: a real-time filter for immediate
state output and a smoother for mapping, delayed corrections, or offline analysis.

The practical concept to remember is **sparsity**. A useful factor graph is not
just a giant dense matrix. Each measurement usually touches only a few states, so
the solver can exploit sparse linear algebra. That is one reason graph methods
scale better than a naive full covariance over every pose and landmark.

## Visual-Inertial Odometry and SLAM

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) estimates motion by combining camera measurements
with IMU measurements. Visual-inertial SLAM extends this with mapping and loop
closure.

The combination works because the sensors fail differently:

| Sensor | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Camera | Rich geometric constraints from the environment | Sensitive to lighting, blur, texture, and scale ambiguity |
| IMU | High-rate short-term motion and gravity information | Bias-driven drift when used alone |

In a modern VIO system, the IMU usually propagates motion between camera frames.
The camera then corrects drift by tracking features, direct photometric patches,
or learned descriptors. Many systems maintain keyframes rather than every image.
Keyframes limit computation while preserving enough history for optimization.

A central idea is **IMU preintegration**. Instead of adding every IMU sample as a
separate graph constraint, the system summarizes many high-rate IMU samples into
a relative motion factor between two keyframes. That factor depends on current
accelerometer and gyro bias estimates, so serious implementations also track the
Jacobian of the preintegrated measurement with respect to those biases.

VIO also exposes observability issues that are easy to miss in simple examples:

- monocular vision alone does not know metric scale;
- gravity direction and accelerometer bias are coupled during initialization;
- pure rotation provides poor translation information;
- weak excitation makes some calibration states hard to estimate;
- camera-IMU time offset can look like bad estimator tuning.

Systems such as MSCKF-style filters, sliding-window bundle adjustment, and
ORB-SLAM-style visual-inertial SLAM all live in this design space. The details
differ, but the recurring pattern is the same: use IMU for high-rate propagation,
vision for environmental constraints, and careful timing/calibration to make the
fusion meaningful.

## Advanced GNSS Processing

GNSS receiver signals, observables, RTK/PPP context, and the boundary between
loose, tight, and deep integration now have a dedicated optional chapter:
[GNSS Signals, Receivers, and Deep Integration](adv-gnss.qmd). The required
course material remains the loose INS/GNSS workflow in the global-navigation
part of the book.

## GNSS-Denied and Resilient Navigation

GNSS-denied navigation means operating when satellite positioning is unavailable,
unreliable, or intentionally attacked. This is common indoors, underwater,
underground, near tall buildings, under foliage, inside warehouses, in combat
environments, and around jamming or spoofing.

No single replacement sensor solves the whole problem. Resilient navigation uses
layers:

| Aid | Useful when | Main weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Visual odometry | Textured scenes and reasonable lighting | Blur, darkness, textureless areas |
| Lidar odometry | Geometric structure is visible | Dust, rain, glass, feature-poor corridors |
| Radar odometry | Weather, dust, smoke, long range | Lower angular resolution and harder data association |
| Terrain-relative navigation | Terrain maps are available | Needs distinctive terrain and good maps |
| Magnetic anomaly navigation | Magnetic maps are available | Local disturbances and map dependence |
| Barometric aiding | Altitude changes matter | Weather and pressure drift |
| Wheel or water-speed aiding | Vehicle-environment contact is reliable | Slip, currents, and calibration |
| Signals of opportunity | Radio infrastructure exists | Opportunistic and environment-dependent |
| Cooperative localization | Other agents are nearby | Communication and shared-frame uncertainty |

The professional habit is graceful degradation. A GNSS-denied system should not
pretend nothing happened. It should change mode, report lower confidence, adjust
controller limits when appropriate, and log enough information to explain the
outage later.

## Advanced SLAM and Mapping

The SLAM module introduced EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, GraphSLAM, visual navigation, and
loop closure. Advanced SLAM systems push those ideas in several directions.

### Dense, Semantic, and Dynamic Maps

Classical feature maps are compact, but they do not describe all occupied space.
Dense mapping attempts to reconstruct surfaces, occupancy, or signed distance
fields. Semantic mapping attaches labels such as road, building, tree, person,
vehicle, buoy, or runway. Dynamic mapping tries to separate persistent structure
from moving objects.

The price is computation and modeling complexity. A dense semantic map is more
useful to a planner than a sparse point cloud, but it is harder to build,
maintain, validate, and update over time.

### Lidar, Radar, and Multi-Modal SLAM

Lidar SLAM is common because range measurements give direct geometric structure.
Radar SLAM is attractive in rain, dust, fog, smoke, and long-range outdoor
operation. Camera systems are inexpensive and information-rich. IMUs provide
high-rate motion. GNSS provides global anchoring when available.

Modern systems often combine several of these:

- visual-inertial odometry for local motion;
- lidar or radar odometry for geometry and robustness;
- GNSS or map priors for global alignment;
- semantic perception for object-level reasoning;
- loop closure for long-term consistency.

The hard part is not drawing the block diagram. The hard part is time alignment,
calibration, outlier rejection, uncertainty modeling, and knowing which sensor to
distrust in a particular environment.

### Lifelong and Multi-Robot SLAM

Lifelong SLAM asks what happens when the same environment changes over days,
months, or years. Multi-robot SLAM asks how multiple agents share maps and
constraints without assuming perfect communication or a shared initial frame.

These topics matter for fleets, warehouses, ports, cities, mines, farms, and
large autonomous survey operations. They also expose practical problems:

- map growth must be bounded;
- old observations may become stale;
- different robots may use different sensors and clocks;
- loop closures can be false but highly influential;
- communication bandwidth is limited;
- privacy and security may constrain what data can be shared.

## Rao-Blackwellized and Hybrid Filters

FastSLAM is a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF). That phrase is worth
remembering beyond the project.

The idea is to sample the hard part of the state and analytically estimate the
conditional part. In FastSLAM, particles represent robot path hypotheses, while
landmarks are estimated with small EKFs conditioned on each particle. This reduces
the dimension that must be sampled directly.

RBPFs appear in other navigation problems:

- sampling discrete mode hypotheses while filtering continuous vehicle state;
- tracking multiple data-association possibilities;
- estimating maps conditioned on trajectory samples;
- combining particle filters with Kalman filters for partially linear systems.

Hybrid methods are attractive when the posterior is not well represented by one
Gaussian but a full particle filter would be too expensive. They are also easy to
misuse. Particle depletion, poor proposals, overconfident likelihoods, and weak
resampling diagnostics can make a hybrid filter look sophisticated while quietly
throwing away the correct hypothesis.

The takeaway is not "use RBPFs everywhere." The takeaway is that marginalization
and conditional structure can make hard estimation problems tractable.

## Learning-Based and Emerging Methods

Machine learning is now part of navigation, but it rarely replaces the entire
navigation stack. More commonly, learned components provide perception,
correspondence, depth, uncertainty estimates, or priors that are fused with
geometric and probabilistic models.

Important emerging directions include:

- **learned visual features**, replacing or augmenting hand-crafted descriptors;
- **learned depth and optical flow**, especially for difficult visual scenes;
- **event cameras**, which report brightness changes at very high temporal
  resolution and are useful for high-speed or high-dynamic-range motion;
- **radar-inertial odometry**, especially for poor weather and degraded visual
  environments;
- **neural implicit maps**, which represent geometry or appearance with neural
  fields rather than explicit landmarks or grids;
- **3D Gaussian and NeRF-style mapping**, which can produce rich scene
  reconstructions but currently raise hard questions about real-time use,
  uncertainty, and safety-critical validation;
- **foundation-model perception**, where large pretrained models provide object,
  scene, or language-conditioned understanding;
- **learned sensor fusion**, where networks estimate measurement confidence,
  reject outliers, or provide learned motion priors.

The caution is straightforward: learned systems can be powerful, but navigation
needs calibrated uncertainty, failure detection, and operational constraints. A
neural network that works beautifully on a benchmark can still fail in exactly the
weather, lighting, vehicle vibration, or terrain that matters to your deployment.

## How to Read the Research Literature

Advanced navigation papers can be difficult to compare because they often differ
in sensors, datasets, compute hardware, initialization assumptions, and failure
conditions. When reading a paper, ask:

- What sensors are actually used?
- Is the method filter-based, smoother-based, learning-based, or a hybrid?
- Does it run online, offline, or in post-processing?
- What assumptions are made about calibration and synchronization?
- Is global drift bounded by GNSS, loop closure, maps, or external truth?
- How does it handle outliers and sensor dropouts?
- What dataset was used, and does it match the target environment?
- Does the method report failures, or only successful sequences?
- Are uncertainty estimates calibrated, or just plotted?
- What computational hardware was required?

Be especially careful with phrases like "real time," "robust," and
"state-of-the-art." They are meaningful only relative to a platform, dataset,
sensor suite, and operating environment.

## Summary

The advanced topics in this chapter are extensions of the same foundations used
throughout the course:

- factor graphs generalize filtering ideas into sparse optimization over many
  states and measurements;
- VIO and visual-inertial SLAM combine high-rate inertial propagation with
  environmental visual constraints;
- advanced GNSS processing uses raw measurements, RTK, PPP, and tighter INS/GNSS
  coupling instead of relying only on receiver position fixes;
- GNSS-denied navigation is a resilience problem, not a single-sensor replacement
  problem;
- advanced SLAM expands from sparse landmarks to dense, semantic, dynamic,
  lifelong, and multi-robot maps;
- RBPFs and hybrid filters exploit conditional structure when one Gaussian or one
  particle cloud is not enough;
- learning-based methods are increasingly important, but they still need
  calibration, uncertainty, and failure monitoring.

You are not expected to implement these systems in this course. You are expected
to recognize the shape of the field: modern navigation is not one algorithm, but a
set of estimation, sensing, optimization, timing, calibration, and validation
choices made under real constraints.
